bib.title: Alita: Generalist Agent Enabling Scalable Agentic Reasoning with Minimal Predefinition and Maximal Self-Evolution

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Alita: Generalist Agent Enabling Scalable Agentic Reasoning with Minimal Predefinition and Maximal Self-Evolution", Jiahao Qiu, Xuan Qi, Tongcheng Zhang et al. (Princeton AI Lab, Tsinghua, SJTU and others; senior author Mengdi Wang), arXiv:2505.20286v1 [cs.AI], 26 May 2025. Preprint. No venue printed.

COVERAGE: all 40,520 chars read, 12 pages. This includes Table 1-4, the Appendix A case study, Appendix B limitations and the references. Figure 1 is chart text only. I did not run the figures script. I did not open the target note beyond its first 60 lines, so I did not check which claims it needs.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The main claim is that Alita is a generalist agent with one core component (a web agent) plus a few general modules. It generates MCP servers on the fly rather than relying on predefined tools. The authors say this works best on GAIA.
  number: 75.15% pass@1, 87.27% pass@3 (GAIA validation)
  setup: Claude-Sonnet-4 manager with GPT-4o. GAIA validation set; the paper describes GAIA as 466 questions. pass@k means running the framework k times and keeping the best answer. Three rounds were run.
  quote: "Alita with Claude-Sonnet-4 and GPT-4o achieves 75.15% pass@1 and 87.27% pass@3 accuracy, which is top-ranking on the GAIA benchmark validation dataset"
  where: p.7, section 4.2
- It beats OpenAI Deep Research and the other baselines on GAIA.
  number: 72.73% pass@1 and 86.06% pass@3 (Claude-3.7-Sonnet + GPT-4o). Baselines: OpenAI-DR 67.36, OWL 69.09, A-World 69.70, AutoAgent 55.15, ODR-smolagents 55.15, Octotools 18.40.
  setup: Table 1 total accuracy. The baseline rows are single figures, with no stated pass@k. Alita is best-of-k. See LIMITS.
  quote: "surpassing OpenAI's Deep Research with 67.36% pass@1 and ranking top among all general-purpose agents"
  where: p.3 (contributions) and Table 1, p.7
- Reusing Alita-generated MCPs raises another agent's score on GAIA.
  number: ODR-smolagents + GPT-4o goes from 27.88% to 33.94% total. Level 3 goes from 11.54% to 15.38%.
  setup: Open Deep Research-smolagents with GPT-4o, with and without the MCPs. The MCPs were collected from Alita runs on the same GAIA set.
  quote: "ODR-smolagents + GPT-4o(No Alita MCPs) 33.96% 29.07% 11.54% 27.88%" and "ODR-smolagents + GPT-4o(With Alita MCPs) 39.62% 36.05% 15.38% 33.94%"
  where: Table 2, p.8
- MCP reuse works as a cheap distillation from a strong model to a weak one.
  number: GPT-4o-mini base framework goes from 21.82% to 29.09% average. Level 3 goes from 3.85% to 11.54%, which the authors call tripling.
  setup: Base framework (ODR-smolagents without the MCP-creation component, plus its predefined tools) on GPT-4o-mini. The MCPs came from Claude-3.7-Sonnet runs on GAIA.
  quote: "Base Framework + GPT-4o-mini (No Alita MCP) 32.08% 20.93% 3.85% 21.82%" and "Base Framework + GPT-4o-mini (With Alita MCP) 39.62% 27.91% 11.54% 29.09%"
  where: Table 3, p.8
  related quote: "the reuse of MCPs generated from agents with larger LLMs is much easier, cheaper, and faster than traditional distillation." (p.7, section 5.1.1)
- Tool generation needs a strong coder model. Alita on GPT-4o-mini generates its own MCPs and scores far lower.
  number: 43.64% total, against 72.73% for Claude-3.7-Sonnet + GPT-4o
  setup: GAIA. Alita with GPT-4o-mini and no pre-distilled MCPs.
  quote: "Alita (GPT-4o-mini) 54.72% 44.19% 19.23% 43.64%"
  where: Table 4, p.9
- The paper gives two secondary results, both on 100 random samples per benchmark.
  number: Mathvista 74% and PathVQA 52% pass@1. Octotools scores 68 and 47. ODR-smolagents scores 65 and 42.
  setup: Claude-3.7-Sonnet + GPT-4o. The authors sampled 100 items from each dataset "Due to limitations in resources".
  quote: "further attains 74.00% and 52.00% pass@1 on the Mathvista and PathVQA benchmarks, respectively"
  where: p.7, Table 1
- The design is a loop with fixed stages. These are the mechanics worth citing for the note.
  number: none
  setup: The manager agent calls three tools: MCP Brainstorming (finds the capability gap and writes a tool spec), ScriptGeneratingTool (writes the script plus an environment script and a cleanup script, guided by GitHub links from the web agent) and CodeRunningTool (runs the script in isolation). The web agent uses SimpleTextBrowser, VisitTool, PageUpTool, PageDownTool, GoogleSearchTool and GithubSearchTool. A tool that works is registered as an MCP in the "MCP Box". Each tool gets its own Conda environment, installed with conda or pip, with no containers. Failed setups trigger fallbacks such as relaxing version constraints. If recovery fails, the tool is discarded and the failure is logged.
  quote: "Upon successful tool generation and accurate result formulation, the corresponding script is transformed into an MCP and stored in the internal tool registry for future reuse."
  where: pp.4-6, sections 3.1-3.4
- Brainstorming exists because models overestimate what they can do.
  number: none
  quote: "Since LLMs often exhibit overconfidence in their capabilities [22], we introduce MCP Brainstorming to conduct preliminary capability assessment"
  where: p.5, section 3.4.1
- MCP creation is claimed to beat plain tool creation on reuse and environment management. This is asserted and not tested.
  number: none
  quote: "Alita enables MCP creation, which provides additional benefits, including better reusability and easy environment management over tool creation."
  where: p.3, section 2.3
- The authors' rationale for predefined toolkits failing: "incomplete coverage", "limited creativity and flexibility", and "mismatch" (many tools are not written in Python). MCP is described as "an open protocol that standardizes how different systems provide context to LLMs".
  where: p.2

LIMITS
- The authors concede one limit: "Alita highly relies on the coding capability of LLM. When the LLM's coding capability is really poor, our method will perform worse than traditional generalist agent." (Appendix B)
- Pass@3 means best of three runs, so it is not comparable with the single-run baselines. Only pass@1 is like for like. Even then the baseline numbers appear to be copied from other sources, and the paper does not say how they were obtained.
- The MCP-reuse experiments (Tables 2 and 3) use MCPs generated while running GAIA and then evaluate on GAIA. The paper does not say whether the questions were held out. This is a possible train/test overlap.
- Mathvista and PathVQA use only 100 samples, with no confidence intervals.
- Single-run results throughout, with no variance reported. Table 1 has no pass@2 or pass@3 for the Mathvista and PathVQA columns.
- No ablation of individual components (Brainstorming, web agent, reuse). No cost, latency or token numbers. No safety analysis, even though the agent downloads and runs GitHub code. The sandbox is only a Conda environment: "without administrative privileges or containerization".
- The paper gives no evidence that the generated tools are real MCP servers in protocol terms. It does not describe a transport, schema or discovery. "MCP" here means a packaged reusable script.
- Model versions are dated: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini. The leaderboard claim "top-ranking" is as of May 2025.
- The text says the "MCP Box" is stored in an "internal tool registry". It does not say how the registry is searched or pruned as it grows.
- The paper only claims a single case study (Appendix A, YouTube subtitle crawler), not a systematic analysis.

BUILDS ON
Open Deep Research / smolagents (Roucher et al., 2025), which Alita is "largely based on", with predefined tools removed and the MCP-creation component added. MCP (Anthropic). RAG-MCP (Gan and Sun, 2025). Tool creation: CRAFT (Yuan et al., 2023), TroVE (Wang, Fried, Neubig, 2024), CREATOR (Qian et al., 2023), AutoAgent (Tang, Fan, Huang, 2025), OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024). Workflow generation: AFlow (Zhang et al., 2024), AutoAgents (Chen et al., 2023). Baselines: OWL (Hu et al., 2025), A-World (Ant Group, 2025), Octotools (Lu et al., 2025), Magentic-One (Fourney et al., 2024), OpenAI Deep Research. Benchmarks: GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), MathVista (Lu et al., 2024), PathVQA (He et al., 2020). Overconfidence: Sun et al., 2025. The name "CodeReAct loop" appears in Figure 3. There is no ReAct citation.

CODE
Appendix A, p.12 (the case study's example MCP):
conda create -n youtube_transcript
conda activate youtube_transcript
pip install youtube-transcript-api
from youtube_transcript_api import YouTubeTranscriptApi
ytt_api = YouTubeTranscriptApi()
transcript_list = ytt_api.list('video_id')

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p.1: GAIA bar chart of Alita, manus.ai and OpenAI DeepResearch by level. Extraction gives numbers only, with no labels, so I could not map them to bars.
- Fig 2, p.3: comparison of traditional generalist agents (many hand-built tools, a manager agent) with Alita (web agent plus MCP creation and a "MCP Box").
- Fig 3, p.4: architecture diagram of the loop. Question goes to MCP Brainstorming, then open-source search, script generation, virtual-environment execution (CodeReAct loop), encapsulation into the MCP Box, then output. It shows the self-evolving cycle faster than the prose.

PROBLEMS
- No instructions embedded in the PDF text.
- Figure 1 text is jumbled. The Table 1 header row ("level1 level2 level3 total") lost its column alignment but the rows are readable.
- Table 1 reports OpenAI-DR level 2 and level 3 as 69.06 and 47.60, but Figure 1 shows 74.3 and 69.1. These are different from each other and I could not tell which fits. The Figure 1 mapping is uncertain.
- The text puts "Alita ... Claude-Sonnet-4 and GPT-4o" as the headline. The Table 1 header calls the other row Claude-3.7-Sonnet, so the 72.73 figure and the 75.15 figure use different manager models.
- The source file is /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/02-context-engineering/sources/qiu-2025-alita.pdf. The note 09-protocols.md currently covers NOCODE prompt shells and says MCP is in note 10. Alita fits note 10 (MCP) better than 09.
